notes: Three adhyāyas, five khaṇḍas, 33 mantras (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4–6): the creation of the worlds and their guardians by the Self and its entry into the body; the three births; and the Self as consciousness. Meanings and translation follow Śaṅkara's bhāṣya.

invocation.translation: Om. My speech is established in my mind; my mind is established in my speech. O manifest one, be manifest to me. You two are the linch-pins of the Veda for me. May what I have heard not forsake me. By this that I have studied I join days and nights. I shall speak what is right; I shall speak what is true. May that protect me; may that protect the speaker. May it protect me, may it protect the speaker, may it protect the speaker. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
notes: The peace invocation of the Upaniṣads of the Ṛgveda, printed at the opening of the e-text. Śaṅkara's Aitareya bhāṣya does not comment on it; the translation gives the plain sense of the words. ‘You two’ are speech and mind; ‘the speaker’ is the teacher. The e-text prints āṇīsthaḥ as one word.

translations.text: In the beginning this was the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatever that winked. He reflected: ‘Let me now create worlds.’

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad: action together with the knowledge of the lower Brahman is finished, and its highest end, the merging in the deity that is called prāṇa, has been summed up through the knowledge of the uktha. Some hold that this merging is the highest human end, that it is liberation, to be reached by knowledge and rites combined, and that there is nothing beyond it. To set them aside the text goes on, ‘the Self, verily …’, to enjoin the knowledge of the Self alone. How is it known that what follows enjoins a knowledge unconnected with action? Because no other purpose is understood; and because it will show that the deities named before, fire and the rest, belong to saṃsāra, having the faults of hunger and the like (1.2.1), while the supreme Brahman is heard to be beyond hunger and the like.

Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad, the objection: granted that the knowledge of the Self alone is the means of liberation; still it is the performer of rites who is entitled to it here, since no other, a man of another āśrama who does no rites, is mentioned, and the knowledge is begun directly after the rite of the thousand bṛhatī verses. Nor is this knowledge unconnected with action, for it ends as the earlier one did: as the brāhmaṇa and the mantra ‘the sun is the self’ (Ṛgveda 1.115.1) said that the man connected with rites, as the sun, is the self of all creatures moving and unmoving, so here ‘this is Brahmā, this is Indra’ ends with ‘all that is led by consciousness’ (3.1.3); the Saṃhitopaniṣad too speaks of him in connection with rites (‘the Bahvṛcas consider him in the great uktha’) and ends ‘in all beings they call him Brahman’. If it is said that settling again, with the question ‘who is this Self?’ (3.1.1), a self already settled is a useless repetition: no, it settles further properties of that same self of the man of rites, the creating, sustaining and withdrawing of the world, or it is for meditation alone; or the self that is seen as different in the sphere of rites is to be meditated on as non-different when no rite is being done. The Vājasaneyins say ‘he who knows knowledge and ignorance, both together …’ (Īśa 11) and ‘only doing works here should one wish to live a hundred years’ (Īśa 2); mortals have no life beyond a hundred years in which to give up action and meditate on the Self; ‘as long as he lives he offers the agnihotra’, ‘they burn him with his sacrificial vessels’, and the text on the three debts say the same. So the texts on wandering mendicancy (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.5.1, 4.4.22) are praise of the knowledge of the Self, or are meant for those not entitled to rites.

Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad, the reply: no; when the highest truth is known and no fruit is seen, action is not possible. One who knows as his Self ‘I am Brahman’, the supreme, whose desires are attained, free of all the faults of saṃsāra, sees no purpose for himself in what is done or to be done. If he acts because he is enjoined: no, for he has seen the Self that is not an object of injunction. He who sees gaining the desired and avoiding the undesired as his purpose and seeks the means is the object of injunction; not he who sees himself as Brahman. If even he were enjoined, no one would be unenjoined and every action would have to be done by everyone always. Nor can he be enjoined by anyone, for the Veda itself issues from him: no one is commanded by words that arise from his own knowledge, nor a wise master by an undiscerning servant. If the Veda, being eternal and independent, can command all, the same fault stands. If the scripture enjoins on the same man both the duty of action and the knowledge of the Self: it cannot teach of one thing what is contradictory, as heat and cold of fire. The wish to gain the desired and avoid the undesired is not made by scripture, for it is seen in all creatures, even cowherds; scripture teaches what is not got of itself. Having produced the knowledge of the Self, which is opposed to anything being left to do, how could it again produce a duty, like cold in fire or darkness in the sun? And it does teach it: ‘let him know: he is my Self’ (Kauṣītaki 3.9), ‘consciousness is Brahman’ (3.1.3), ‘it knew only itself’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4), ‘you are that’ (Chāndogya 6.8–16). The knowledge of Brahman as the Self, once arisen, is not sublated, so it cannot be called unarisen or mistaken.

Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad, on renunciation: if it is said that giving up action is equally without purpose (‘nor has he anything to gain here by what is not done’, Gītā 3.18): no, for renunciation (vyutthāna) is merely not acting. That there is a purpose is caused by ignorance and is not a property of the thing; activity of speech, mind and body is seen in one driven by thirst for a purpose; wife, sons, wealth and the rest, the fivefold, are all objects of desire (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.17), ‘both these are desires only’ (3.5.1, 4.4.22). In the knower, who lacks the faults of ignorance and desire, such activity cannot arise; renunciation is the mere absence of action, not something positive to be performed like a sacrifice. It is the property of the man of knowledge, so no purpose need be sought: one does not ask what purpose is served when a man who walked in the dark does not fall into pit, mud and thorns once the light has risen. If, then, the knower may stay in the householder's state without acting: no, that state is prompted by desire; renunciation is the mere absence of the fixed tie with sons, wealth and the like. Hence service of the teacher and austerity also are not binding on the knower. Some householders, afraid of begging and of contempt, argue that the mendicant too keeps rules of begging, so the householder who wants only to keep the body alive, free of both desires, may stay at home on bare food and clothing. No: holding to a particular house of one's own is prompted by desire; and without it he is in fact a mendicant. If, as the mendicant keeps rules in begging and in purity, the knowing householder should keep to the daily rites because they are enjoined for life: this was answered, the knower is not an object of injunction and cannot be enjoined. The lifelong injunctions are not thereby useless: they hold for those who do not know. The regularity of the mendicant's activity for the bare upkeep of the body is not what prompts it, as the going of thirst is not the purpose of one who sips water for purification; and it continues from earlier habit, since to break it would cost effort.

Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad, the conclusion: because renunciation, though it follows of itself, is stated again, the knower must take to it; and one who does not yet know but seeks liberation must also take to wandering mendicancy: ‘calm, restrained’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.23), for calm, restraint and the other means of seeing the Self are not possible in the other āśramas; ‘to those beyond the āśramas he taught the supreme purifier’ (Śvetāśvatara 6.21); ‘not by action, not by offspring or wealth, by renunciation some reached immortality’ (Kaivalya 2). The highest fruit of the householder's rites and the knowledge that goes with them has been summed up as merging in the deity, which is within saṃsāra; had the knowledge of the supreme Self belonged to the man of rites, the summing up would not have been of such a fruit. Nor is that a subordinate fruit, for the knowledge that leads to immortality has for its object the Self in which all name, form and action are negated (‘where all has become his very Self’ against ‘where there is duality, as it were’, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.14). The bar of the debts holds only for one who does not know, for gaining the worlds of men, fathers and gods (1.5.16); for the knower who seeks the world of the Self there is none: ‘what shall we do with offspring’ (4.4.22), the Kāvaṣeya seers, and the Kauṣītakins' ‘the ancients who knew did not offer the agnihotra’ (2.5). Nor do debts bar the unknowing seeker from mendicancy: before he becomes a householder there is no debt, and ‘let him go forth from home, having become a forest-dweller, or else from studentship itself’ (Jābāla 4). Mendicancy is not for the unqualified only; they are spoken of separately. To do as one likes is quite out of the question for the knower, for that belongs to the deluded; even enjoined action is felt by him as a heavy burden. ‘Knowledge and ignorance together’ (Īśa 11) does not mean that both are in one man at one time, any more than the knowledge of silver and of the shell in the shell: ‘far apart and opposed are ignorance and what is known as knowledge’ (Kaṭha 1.2.4). Austerity, service of the teacher and the like, the means by which knowledge arises, are called ignorance because they are action; by them he brings forth knowledge and crosses death, that is desire, and then, desireless, reaches immortality by the knowledge of Brahman. ‘A hundred years’ (Īśa 2) holds for one who does not know. So what follows is begun to show the knowledge of the actionless Brahman alone as one's Self.

Śaṅkara: ātman is from āp (to pervade), ad (to eat) or at (to go on always): the supreme, all-knowing, all-powerful, free of hunger and every property of saṃsāra, by nature eternally pure, awake and free, unborn, undecaying, deathless, immortal, fearless, without a second. ‘This’, the world divided by name, form and action, was the Self alone before the creation. Is it not he alone now? It is; but there is a difference. Before its origin the world, its names and forms unmanifest, one with the Self, was the object of the one word and idea ‘Self’; now, its names and forms manifest, it is the object of many words and ideas and of the one word ‘Self’ as well: as foam, before its name and form are set apart from water, is the object of the one word ‘water’, and afterwards of both. ‘Nothing else that winked’: nothing active, or anything else; unlike the independent pradhāna of the Sāṃkhyas, which stands apart from the Self, or the atoms of the followers of Kaṇāda. How could he reflect before the creation, having no body or organs? By his all-knowing nature: ‘without hands or feet he is swift and grasps’ (Śvetāśvatara 3.19). ‘Worlds’: Ambhas and the rest, the places where creatures experience the fruits of their actions.

translations.text: He created these worlds: Ambhas, the Marīcis, Mara and the Āpas. That Ambhas is beyond heaven; heaven is its support. The Marīcis are the mid-region. Mara is the earth. Those that are below are the Āpas.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: having so reflected.

Śaṅkara: as a skilled carpenter here thinks ‘let me make a palace of such a kind’ and then makes it. But the carpenter has material; how does the Self create worlds without material? There is no fault: name and form, unmanifest and one with the Self, denoted by the one word ‘Self’, are the material of the manifest world, as water is of foam. Or rather, as a knowing magician, without material, projects himself as another self that seems to walk in the sky, so the all-knowing god, all-powerful, of great māyā, projects himself as another, in the form of the world; this is the more fitting, and so the views that the effect, or the cause, or both are non-existent find no place. Having brought forth the egg in the order beginning with space, he created the worlds, which the text itself explains. Ambhas, beyond heaven, is so called because it bears water; heaven is its support. The mid-region below heaven is the Marīcis: plural, though one, because of its many places, or from its connection with the rays (marīci). The earth is Mara, because beings die (mriyante) in it. Those below the earth are the Āpas, from āp (to reach). Though the worlds are made of the five elements, they are called by names of water because water predominates in them.

translations.text: He reflected: ‘Here now are the worlds; let me now create guardians of the worlds.’ Having drawn out from the waters themselves a Puruṣa, (a form like a man,) he gave it shape.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: having created the four worlds, which are the seats where all creatures take the fruits of their actions.

Śaṅkara: the Lord reflected again: these worlds I have created would perish without protectors, so let me create guardians to protect them. ‘From the waters’: from the five elements in which water predominates, the same from which he created Ambhas and the other worlds. ‘A Puruṣa’: of the shape of a man, with head, hands and the rest. He drew it out as a potter takes a lump of clay from the earth, and massed it together by joining its own limbs.

padaccheda.deva: तम् अभ्यतपत् तस्य अभितप्तस्य मुखम् निरभिद्यत यथा अण्डम् मुखात् वाक् वाचः अग्निः नासिके निरभिद्येताम् नासिकाभ्याम् प्राणः प्राणात् वायुः अक्षिणी निरभिद्येताम् अक्षीभ्याम् चक्षुः चक्षुषः आदित्यः कर्णौ निरभिद्येताम् कर्णाभ्याम् श्रोत्रम् श्रोत्रात् दिशः त्वक् निरभिद्यत त्वचः लोमानि लोमभ्यः ओषधि-वनस्पतयः हृदयम् निरभिद्यत हृदयात् मनः मनसः चन्द्रमाः नाभिः निरभिद्यत नाभ्याः अपानः अपानात् मृत्युः शिश्नम् निरभिद्यत शिश्नात् रेतः रेतसः आपः

grammar.en: past passive participle m. gen. sg.

translations.text: He brooded over him. Of him who was so brooded over the mouth burst forth, like an egg; from the mouth speech, from speech fire. The nostrils burst forth; from the nostrils prāṇa, from prāṇa air. The eyes burst forth; from the eyes sight, from sight the sun. The ears burst forth; from the ears hearing, from hearing the quarters. The skin burst forth; from the skin the hairs, from the hairs herbs and trees. The heart burst forth; from the heart the mind, from the mind the moon. The navel burst forth; from the navel apāna, from apāna death. The generative organ burst forth; from the generative organ seed, from seed the waters.

notes: Śaṅkara: ‘he brooded over’ that lump of the shape of a man: he thought on it, he formed a resolve, as in ‘whose austerity consists of knowledge’ (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9). Heated by that austerity, the Lord's resolve, an opening of the shape of a mouth arose in the lump, as a bird's egg bursts. From the mouth came forth the organ of speech, and from speech fire, the guardian who presides over it. So in every case three burst forth in order: the seat, the organ, and the deity. The heart is the seat of the inner organ; the mind is the inner organ. The navel is the place where all the prāṇas are bound; ‘apāna’ means the organ of excretion, because it is joined with apāna, and death is the deity that presides over it. The generative organ is the seat of the organ of generation; the organ itself is called ‘seed’ together with the seed, since it serves to emit it.
